# Independent audit: arbitrary-body normal variations and convex-order stress

Auditor: research-agent. Date: 2026-09-19.



This theorem supplies no OC constant. The arbitrary finite-base (gamma_d/h(P)) target is false, and the conditions may hold at its genuine below-target minima. The inherited complete affine lattice and occupied-parity budget must be retained in an OC application. The source explicitly restricts the boundary-area argument to (d\ge1) and positive (d)-dimensional fibers.

## 1. Supports and actual variations

For the hull of the finite fiber family, taking support in a fixed continuous direction commutes with the convex combinations defining a section. Thus the stated finite linear program

\[
h_z(u)=\max\{\sum_p\alpha_ph_p(u):\alpha\ge0,
 \sum_p\alpha_p=1,\ \sum_p\alpha_pp=z\}
\]

is exact, including boundary bases. Its value is a concave polyhedral roof in (z). The affine coefficients arising from the finitely many possible independent support subsets are bounded uniformly as (u) varies on the sphere, since the base is fixed and all (h_p(u)) are bounded. Consequently the roofs are uniformly Lipschitz in (z) on the base polytope. Together with their uniform Lipschitz dependence on (u), from the bounded continuous fiber region, this justifies the stated joint continuity. No common optimal basis for all (u) is needed; the maximizing basis can change.

Selecting an inner ball in each measured fiber and taking weighted centers gives a ball of one common positive radius in every real section. Uniform boundedness also follows from the finite source hull.

In the variation

\[
u\cdot x+\varepsilon V(u,z,x)\le h_z(u)\quad(|u|=1),
\]

the left side is convex in the physical variables for each fixed (u), and the right side is concave. Their intersection is therefore a convex set with its stated sections exactly. For a finite list of convex potentials, affine minorants and compactness in (u,z) give

\[
V(u,z,x)\ge-L(1+|x|).
\]

Testing (u=x/|x|) bounds the entire perturbed body, before any appeal to local uniform convergence. Smaller fixed interior balls then survive for small (arepsilon). Signed normal-dependent affine directions and nonnegative convex-potential coefficients are jointly feasible by this same single construction. There is no subsequent convexification of independently changed fibers.

## 2. Radial first variation without smoothness

On the now-bounded variation region, (V) is uniformly bounded. Support inequalities sandwich each perturbed fiber between inner and outer parallel bodies at distances (O(\varepsilon)). About a fixed interior ball center, these bodies lie between homotheties with ratios (1+O(\varepsilon)) and (1-O(\varepsilon)). The radial functions therefore differ by (O(\varepsilon)) uniformly.

At an original regular radial endpoint (x=c+\rho\omega), the support normal (u_0) is unique. Compactness of the normal parameter gives an active normal (u_\varepsilon) at the perturbed radial endpoint. Any limit of these normals supports (x), hence equals (u_0). Also (u_0\cdot\omega\ge r_0/R_0>0). Testing the new point with (u_0) gives the upper bound on its difference quotient. The active (u_\varepsilon) equation and the nonnegative original support slack give the lower bound. Both yield

\[
\rho'(0+)=-\frac{V(u_0,p,x)}{u_0\cdot\omega}.
\]

The radial parametrization and inverse are Lipschitz, so the exceptional nonregular boundary set has a null set of directions. Dominated convergence and the radial surface Jacobian give

\[
M'(0+)=\int r\,d\eta,\qquad r=-V.
\]

The (d=1) case is the two endpoint derivative with counting surface measure. No (d=0) claim is made. The fixed-cap indicator argument is valid when the cap plane has zero fiber-boundary surface measure; the source explicitly replaces it at coincident facets.

## 3. Cap signs and consistent allocations

For a cap (a\cdot z+v\cdot x\ge b) with (|v|=1), let

\[
\ell=\delta a\cdot z+\delta v\cdot x-\delta b.
\]

On a proper section the moving-cap flux is (+\int\ell\,d\mathcal H_{d-1}). At a coincident inside facet, the fiber outward normal is (-v); outward distance (	au) belongs to the cap iff (	au\le\varepsilon\ell+o(\varepsilon)). Combining with the moved body boundary (	au\le\varepsilon r+o(\varepsilon)) gives (min(r,\ell)). At a coincident outside facet the outward normal is (v), the cap is (	au\ge-\varepsilon\ell+o(\varepsilon)), and the added thickness is (max(r+\ell,0)). These signs remain valid for negative offsets and either sign of velocity.

The appropriate linear allocations are therefore

\[
\alpha r+\sigma\ell,quad
\alpha+\sigma=1\quad\hbox{(inside)},\qquad
\alpha=\sigma\in[0,1]\quad\hbox{(outside)}.
\]

The same (alpha,\sigma) must be used in the body and section terms. For an inside facet, *every* preassigned measurable (alpha\in[0,1]) yields the required upper bound on the actual minimum. Outside facets require the supremum over the allowed allocations. Thus fixing arbitrary inside allocations does not invalidate the subsequent descent test.

Proper sections and relative interiors of coincident facets account for all first-order terms. Their omitted boundaries have zero relevant surface measure. The surface measure of other boundary points in a shrinking cap-plane neighborhood tends to zero, while displacement is uniformly (O(\varepsilon)), giving the remaining (o(\varepsilon)) error.

The finite critical-cover dependency uses actual families. Its interior-anchor assertion is justified by the archived minimal-base-face support argument: a fiber-boundary point admits a relative supporting functional with nonzero continuous part on that face; a sufficiently large finite exposing base functional removes off-face fibers. Its raw depth is zero. Positive restricted maxima are consequently interior, and the archived attained-cap/active-normal argument supplies finite positive circuits there. In particular every selected critical cap has a positive proper own section and a positive-area own-boundary patch strictly inside it.

Under common erosion (r=-1), fixed cap parameters, every allocated cap gradient is therefore at most a fixed negative constant. Both kinds of coincident allocations are nonpositive and cannot cancel that strict inside-patch contribution. This verifies the common strict direction used in separation.

## 4. Cone separation and the exact multiplier sum

For a fixed finite set of body directions and cap-parameter directions, the cap gradient sets are compact and convex: their variable facet densities lie in ([0,1]), and only finitely many continuous moments are evaluated. The exact circuit constraints are linear in cap velocities, preserve continuous-normal balance, and retain every active covering margin. The allowed cone (D) is closed and convex; originally strict cover margins persist locally.

Let (e) denote common erosion. If

\[
w_m=\sum_j\lambda_{m,j}g_{m,j}+\ell_m,
\quad\lambda_{m,j}\ge0,\quad\ell_m\in D^\circ,
\]

converges, pairing with (e\in D) gives

\[
w_m(e)\le-c\sum_j\lambda_{m,j},\qquad c>0.
\]

Thus the nonnegative coefficients are bounded. Compactness of the gradient sets and closedness of the polar then prove closure of their conic sum. This is sufficient for the separation step; no unproved closed-cone sum rule is used.

If the objective (L_0) were outside that sum, separation would produce (delta\in D) with (L_0(\delta)>0) and every candidate cap derivative at most zero. Adding a small positive multiple of (e) makes every such bound strictly negative while keeping (L_0>0). The actual feasible family then has larger total mass and all critical cap budgets strictly below the old (Q). Whole-plane coverage and the fixed slack covers yield a strict depth decrease. This contradicts the assumed unrestricted local minimum and proves the stated certificate with objective coefficient one.

For the signed dilation direction, use

\[
r=u\cdot x,\qquad\delta v_j=0,\quad
\delta a_j=a_j,\quad\delta b_j=b_j.
\]

Both signs satisfy every active cone constraint. The support construction realizes this velocity (it need not be the exact finite dilation path). On a proper cap section (ell_j=-v_j\cdot x). On an inside coincidence (r=\ell_j), and on an outside coincidence (r+\ell_j=0). The divergence identity therefore gives, for *every* consistent allocation,

\[
L_0=dM,\qquad g_j=dQ.
\]

The polar vanishes on this signed direction, giving exactly

\[
\sum_j\lambda_j=M/Q=1/\beta.
\]

## 5. One certificate for all tests

The multiplier normalization places (lambda) in a fixed compact simplex. Store (lambda_j\alpha_j) and (lambda_j\sigma_j) as measures on each fixed coincident facet. Their domination by (lambda_j\mathcal H_{d-1}|_F), the inside-sum relation, and the outside-equality relation are weakly closed. Proper-section and strict-boundary contributions are fixed measures multiplied by (lambda_j). This gives one compact certificate space independent of the number of body tests.

Test integrands are continuous on the compact full supporting-normal bundle. On a coincident facet the normal is fixed, so the same is true of each continuous moment of the stored measures. Consequently finite-test identities and inequalities are closed constraints. The certificate for the finite union of any lists proves the finite-intersection property. Compactness supplies a single certificate for all lists, for the fixed chosen circuit cover and any fixed prescribed inside allocations. This does not assert a common certificate for different circuit covers.

Writing (W=\eta-\nu), a signed affine physical test has zero polar pairing and gives (int\psi(u)A(z,x)\,dW=0). A one-sided convex-potential direction has (r=-\psi\Phi), so

\[
-\int\psi\Phi\,dW=\ell(\delta)\le0.
\]

The resulting inequality is therefore (int\psi\Phi\,dW\ge0), with the correct sign. Constant tests give equal total masses, and affine tests give equal first moments. The claimed normal-localized convex order follows as stated.

## 6. The simpler global-margin route

The function (m(z,x)=\inf_{|u|=1}(h_z(u)-u\cdot x)) is concave: its hypograph is the intersection of the hypographs of concave functions. Thus (m\ge\varepsilon\Phi) is convex for convex (Phi), with the same actual-fiber and velocity argument. Inside a section, (m) is the minimum support distance; outside, (-m=\max_u(u\cdot x-h_z(u))) equals the distance to the section by the nearest-point supporting plane. These identities are consistent, but concavity does not depend on them.

The finite-test separation with global physical convex functions gives global physical convex order. Passing from that order to a normal-preserving martingale coupling is a separate theorem, independently assigned to Minkowski. The more general normal-dependent construction already establishes Sections 1--6 directly, so the core certificate does not circularly rely on that coupling.

No step above requires polyhedrality, smoothness, an unproved smoothing limit, or deletion of positive boundary-facet contributions. The theorem remains a necessary stress identity, and the gamma constant does not enter it.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
